Testimony from fewer than four renders the evidence invalid, and the complainant and witnesses may all be charged as liars, with the ḥadd of qadhf, the punishment for false accusation, falling on them for falsely accusing a Muslim. Sūrat an-Nūr says plainly that those who cannot produce four witnesses are liars (24:2). The severity is a shield. It stands so that a husband, a mother-in-law, a co-wife or a sister cannot level accusations out of personal spite, and no ill-wisher gets a channel for private hostility. Some revered elders gave another reason for the number four: the case involves two individuals, the man and the woman, so one case carries the purview of two, and as each requires two witnesses, four are necessary.

**"If they testify, confine the offenders to their homes"** was the first ruling. At the beginning of Islam the woman whose guilt was proven by sufficient evidence was confined to her house, kept from leaving, prevented from mixing with people, and that until death. No release was foreseen except one: **"until they die or Allah ordains a ˹different˺ way for them"**. The way referred to is the abrogation that came later. Ibn ʿAbbās said that confinement was the early ruling, and that it stood until Sūrat an-Nūr came down and replaced it with flogging for fornication and stoning for adultery. The same explanation is reported from ʿIkrimah and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from al-Ḥasan and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ and Zayd ibn Aslam, from Qatādah and ad-Daḥḥāk, and the matter is agreed upon. This hadith of abrogation is the settled understanding of the verse. Interpreting the word "way" itself, Ibn ʿAbbās said it means stoning for the married and lashing for the unmarried, which al-Bukhārī records in the Book of Tafsīr of his Ṣaḥīḥ.

### The way that was ordained

The promised way came from the Prophet's ﷺ own mouth. Imam Aḥmad recorded from ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit that when revelation descended on the Messenger of Allah ﷺ it would weigh on him and his face would show the strain. One day revelation came down, and when he was relieved of its strain he said:

> Take from me: Allah has made some other way for them. The married with the married, the unmarried with the unmarried. The married gets a hundred lashes and stoning to death, while the unmarried gets a hundred lashes then banishment for a year.

Muslim and the collectors of the Sunan recorded from ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit the same instruction, opening with the words: "Take from me, take from me. Allah has made some other way for them." At-Tirmidhī graded the hadith ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

The way was applied. The Prophet ﷺ pronounced the ḥadd of zinā on Māʿiz ibn Mālik and on a woman of the tribe of Azd. Both were married, and both were stoned. A couple among the Jews of Madinah were also stoned, on a judgement pronounced by the authority of an injunction of the Torah. For the unmarried, the Qur'an itself gives the rule in Sūrat an-Nūr: the fornicator, woman or man, receives a hundred lashes (24:2). As for stoning, a verse of the Qur'an was revealed to cover it whose recitation was later abrogated while the injunction itself remained operative. ʿUmar said:

> Surely, Allah sent Muḥammad ﷺ with the truth and sent down to him the Book. In what Allah revealed there was the verse of rajm. The Holy Prophet ﷺ stoned and we stoned after him, and the revealed injunction of rajm stands proved against everyone who commits zinā despite being married, whether man or woman.

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record it, as cited in the Mishkāt.

### The veil over sins

Read inwardly, the four witnesses are a mercy. To lower the veil of generosity over the sins of servants, Allah made the allowance of an excessive number of witnesses for proving lewdness. Following the witnessing procedure of the Law makes establishing proof nearly impossible. When Māʿiz came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of God, may the blessings of God be upon you, I have committed fornication," he answered: maybe you only kissed. On another occasion he told them to smell the man's breath. In this is the strongest proof of how the Law prefers to keep the veil lowered over ugly acts.

### In short

- The charge of zinā against a woman requires four male witnesses of good standing, and any shortfall turns the accusation back on the accusers as the sin of qadhf.
- The house-confinement of this verse was the first-period ruling, and it was abrogated by the way Allah ordained: a hundred lashes and a year's banishment for the unmarried, a hundred lashes and stoning for the married.
- The cases of Māʿiz ibn Mālik and the woman of Azd applied the ruling, and ʿUmar testified that the injunction of stoning stands by revelation even though its recitation was abrogated.
- Read inwardly, the near-impossibility of proof is deliberate: the Law would rather veil a sin than broadcast it.

16.text:
The companion verse moves from the woman accused to the pair who commit the act: "And the two among you who commit this sin—discipline them. If they repent and mend their ways, relieve them. Surely Allah is ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful". Like the verse before it, its ruling was later replaced by the fixed punishments. What it adds is the frame around punishment: discipline, then relief, then the doors of repentance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And the two among you who commit this sin"** uses a dual masculine pronoun, and the grammar opened a real question. One reading takes the two as an unmarried man and woman guilty of adultery, since masculine expressions in general usage include the feminine, and this is the view of al-Shāfī. Mujāhid said the verse was revealed about the case of two men who do it, the act of the people of Lūṭ, and judging by the dual masculine pronoun this is the more obvious sense: the two suffer the same punishment, both are called to repent, both are to be left alone afterward, all of which fits two men, given that for women the verse before has stipulated confinement. Qāḍī Thanāʾullāh Panīpatī is among those who hold the two-males reading. Both readings remain possible.

**"discipline them"** names the first-period penalty, and no fixed method is prescribed. Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said the punishment includes cursing and shaming them and beating them with sandals, verbal reproach together with physical disgrace. The statement is illustrative rather than exhaustive. The whole matter was left to the discretion of the authorities, and the ruling stood only until Allah abrogated it with flogging or stoning. If the sin meant is the act of the people of Lūṭ, the abrogation applies there too in the view of al-Shāfī, though he held that the one who is the object of the act is flogged and banished, not stoned, even if he is married.

**"If they repent and mend their ways"** comes after the punishment in the order of the verse, and the letter fa', "then", carries the sequence. So the repentance does not absolve them of the punishment. What it ends is the disgrace afterward. **"relieve them"** means: stop reproaching them. Whoever truly repents is like the one who has no sin. Where repentance is absent, reproach may continue even after punishment.

**"Surely Allah is ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful"** is the seal. The two Ṣaḥīḥs record the Prophet's ﷺ words: "When the slave-girl of one of you commits illegal sexual intercourse, let him flog her and not chastise her afterwards," because the lashes she receives erase the sin she committed.

### The act of the people of Lūṭ

If the verse does concern two men, the material gathered around it belongs here. The prohibition is of the severest order. Abū Hurairah narrates that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> Allah has cursed seven types of His creatures from above the seven heavens. He has cursed one of them thrice, and cursed the others once, which is enough for them. Of the one cursed thrice He has said: Cursed is he who did what the people of Lūṭ did. Cursed is he who did what the people of Lūṭ did. Cursed is he who did what the people of Lūṭ did.

It is recorded in the At-Targhīb wat-Tarhīb. Abū Hurairah also reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that four types of people begin their day under the wrath of Allah and reach their evening under His rage: men who imitate women, women who imitate men, the one who goes unto animals, and the one who goes unto men. Ibn ʿAbbās narrates the ruling: if you find someone doing what the people of Lūṭ did, kill both the doer and the one to whom it is done, and the collectors of the Sunan record the same from him in the Prophet's ﷺ words.

The first generation treated it as a crime with no precedent except one. The event is related on the authority of Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir: Khālid ibn al-Walīd wrote to Abū Bakr that in a certain Arabian locality there was a man with whom they were doing what is done with women. Abū Bakr called a meeting of the Companions, ʿAlī among them, who said that no human group had committed such a sin except one, and all knew how Allah had dealt with that people. He proposed that the man be condemned to the fire. The Companions concurred, and Abū Bakr decreed it. Four caliphs after him, ʿAlī, ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr and Hishām ibn ʿAbdul-Malik, condemned the guilty to fire. Muslim jurists differ on the fixed punishment, the details standing in the books of fiqh, but the punishments they report are of the utmost severity: burning, bashing under a felled wall, throwing down from a height, stoning, and beheading with the sword.

The reference is to the people to whom Lūṭ (Lot) was sent as prophet. Beyond their disbelief and their ascribing of partners to Allah, they were addicted to this unnatural practice, and when his teaching had no effect on them, the angels, as commanded by Allah, lifted their habitations off the ground, turned them upside down, and threw the whole thing back down.

### The same prohibition within marriage

Other narrations carry warnings against the unnatural act with women. Ibn ʿAbbās narrates that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah does not look with mercy on the person who commits anal intercourse with a man or a woman. Khuzaimah ibn Thābit reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: Allah does not get embarrassed by stating the truth, said three times, and then: do not go unto women anally. Abū Hurairah narrates: cursed is he who goes unto women anally, recorded in the At-Targhīb wat-Tarhīb. He also narrates that whoever approaches a woman in her menses or in her anus, or consults a soothsayer and believes his talk of the unseen, has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muḥammad ﷺ.

### The spirit of the two verses

The deeper law under both verses is the rule of law itself. A man or woman who commits an act considered a sin under Islamic tenets is dealt with under rules, not arbitrarily. It is unjust to name anyone a criminal before the legal conditions are satisfied, and even a proven offender may not be dealt with by summary violence. Punishment exists to carry justice, and justice is never carried by tyranny. Where the sinner pleads guilty and reforms, a sympathetic and forgiving attitude becomes essential. No one should be measured by his past. When God Himself pardons the sincerely repentant and turns in benevolence to those who reform, mere mortals hold no right to taunt former delinquents, and the taunter may yet prove a transgressor himself. Even the command to punish is, read inwardly, the kindest form of counsel: it warns the servant off the act so that he stays on his guard and never becomes deserving of the greater punishment.

### In short

- The pair in the verse are read either as a fornicating man and woman or as two males, the act of the people of Lūṭ, and both readings are argued from the dual masculine pronoun.
- The discipline commanded, reproach, shaming and beating with sandals, was left to the authorities and later abrogated by the fixed punishments of flogging and stoning.
- Repentance after punishment ends the disgrace, not the penalty, and the one who truly repents is as one who has no sin. The flogged slave-girl is not to be chastised afterward.
- If the verse concerns the act of the people of Lūṭ, the prohibition around it is of the utmost severity, from the thrice-repeated curse to the burning decreed by Abū Bakr, and it covers the unnatural act within marriage as well.
- Under all readings, the standing law is proportion and process: no punishment without legal proof, and no taunting of the reformed.

17.text:
Repentance has just been mentioned at the end of the previous verse, and the two verses that follow now set its conditions: "Allah only accepts the repentance of those who commit evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺ then repent soon after—Allah will pardon them. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise". The verse names who may be forgiven, how quickly they must turn, and what the pardon rests on. Its companion verse, coming next, will name those whose turning comes too late.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who commit evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺"** does not mean sins committed by accident. Read plainly, the words could suggest that only the unintentional sin is forgiven and the deliberate one is not. The explanation given by the Companions closes that door. The ignorance here is not unawareness that the act is a sin, nor the absence of intention. It is the heedlessness toward the evil end of sin and its ultimate punishment that gives a person the audacity to venture into it, even while knowing it as sin and approaching it with full volition. The word means carelessness, stupidity.

**"then repent soon after"** sets the time. The limit was drawn by the Prophet ﷺ himself, as the hadith below shows, and the scholars read every stage of life inside it.

**"Allah will pardon them. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"** closes the promise. He is Knowing of His creatures and Wise in what He does with them, accepting the repentance before death and refusing it in the pangs of death.

### Every sin is committed in ignorance

The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say that every sin a servant commits, he commits out of ignorance, and they agreed that every sin committed by intention or otherwise is committed in ignorance. Mujāhid, the master of exegesis, said that everyone who disobeys Allah is, for that matter, ignorant while doing it, even if on the outside he appears to be a person of great learning. Ibn ʿAbbās said it is because of one's ignorance that one commits the error. ʿAbdur-Razzāq and Maʿmar carried the same from Qatādah, and Ibn Jurayj reported it from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ as well.

The Qur'an itself uses the word this way. The brothers of Yūsuf (Joseph) are addressed as the ignorant ones, in verse 89 of that surah, though what they did to him they did knowingly and with full deliberation, not by error or forgetfulness. They are called ignorant because of their heedlessness toward the evil end of their act.

Abū Ḥayyān, in his al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, adds the hadith that a person who commits zinā does not do so while in a state of being a true Muslim. At the moment he succumbs to the temptation, he is flung far from the demand of his faith. ʿIkrimah said that everything done in this mortal world beyond the bounds of obedience to Allah is ignorance. The logic is plain. Whoever disobeys Allah is trading punishment that lasts forever for pleasures that vanish, and no one who makes that exchange can be called rational or smart. The conclusion is a consensus of the entire Muslim ummah: the repentance of a person who commits a sin deliberately can also be accepted.

### How late is "soon after"?

The interpretations all run in one direction. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that it means until just before the person looks at the angel of death. Ad-Daḥḥāk said everything before death is "soon after". Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said it is just before the last breath leaves the throat. ʿIkrimah said all of this life is "soon after". Imam Aḥmad recorded from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as the soul does not reach the throat.

At-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah collected it, and at-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan gharīb. Ibn Mājah's chain names ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, which is a slip, for the correct narrator is ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. Ibn Marduwayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say that a believing servant who repents a month before his death, or a day or a moment earlier, will have his repentance accepted, provided it is genuine and sincere.

So virtually the whole of a person's lifetime falls inside "soon after". The exception is spelled out by the next verse: repentance in the throes of death is not accepted. One scholar of the later generations divided the approach of death into two states. In the first, medicines and efforts have failed and the person knows death is near, but the soul has not yet begun its departure. This is still within "soon after", and repentance here is accepted. In the second, the rattling sound rises from the throat and the pangs of the soul's withdrawal begin, a state of total despair in which the angels and the things of the Hereafter may already be appearing to the dying person. That state is outside "soon after". The addition of "soon after" in this verse is itself a sermon: a person's span is short, and the death he thinks far away may be quite near.

The acceptance is a promise Allah has taken upon Himself, and His promise is certain of fulfilment. In truth He owes nothing to anyone, and the relenting is pure bounty.

### What repentance is

Repentance is not the uttering of words. It is the intense realization of wrongdoing, an agonizing condition on a par with self-punishment, and one who repents from fear of his Lord is surely pardoned. The root of it is that the wrongdoer turns to his Lord so that the Lord turns to him. The one who repents is like a man who, after straying far away, returns home.

Imam al-Ghazālī, in his Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm ad-Dīn, identified three stations regarding sin. The first is total sinlessness, the hallmark of the angels and the prophets. The second belongs to one who ventures into sin, repeats it and persists in it, never ashamed, never thinking of stopping: the degree of the satans and the devils. The third belongs to human beings, the children of Ādam (Adam), who immediately after sinning regret it and resolve firmly never to return. Failing to repent after sin is the style of devils exclusively, and it is the consensus of the ummah that tawbah, repentance, is obligatory: "O those who believe, repent before Allah" (66:8).

Genuine repentance stands on three pillars. First, regret and shame over what was done, for the hadith says tawbah is another name for remorse. Second, immediately leaving the sin and firmly resolving to stay away from it in the future. Third, making amends for what has gone: a missed prayer or fast is made up through qada, the compensatory worship, and one who has lost count should estimate it and offer the qada in all seriousness, even if that means offering, with each ṣalāh due at its time, one qada of every prayer missed in a lifetime. Unpaid zakah is paid for the previous years, all at once or gradually. A usurped right is returned, and a hurt person is asked for forgiveness. Without these, the word "repent" said a thousand times is no repentance. A Persian poet put it delightfully:

> Repentance on the lips, rosary in hand and a heart full of the taste of sin. Sin laughs at my style of seeking forgiveness.

And if a servant falls again out of human weakness, he renews the repentance at once, in the hope that this time, like every other time, the Most-Forgiving will relent toward him. Another couplet says:

> This is the Court of My Presence, not the Court of Despair. Even if you have broken your repentance a hundred times, come again!

How generous is that mercy. A person may spend a lifetime disobeying, and on turning sincerely before death, is not only forgiven but admitted among the favoured servants of Allah and made an inheritor of Paradise. A hadith says the one who repents from sin is loved by Allah, and the one who has repented is like one who never committed the sin. According to some narrations, when repentance finds acceptance, the written record of the sin is erased from the book of deeds, so that on the Day the servant is not disgraced either.

### The inner reading

Read inwardly, tawbah is the road's mark, the leader into the court, the key that opens the treasure, the intercessor that ushers in union, the first of every happiness and the foundation of freedom. Its order is regret first in the heart, then the tongue's apology, and after that the cutting away from evil things and evil company. The report is severe on half-measures: the one who repents but keeps his bad friends has not repented, nor the one who will not put aside excess food and drink, nor the one who will not leave his bed and empty his eyes of sleep, nor the one who will not spend the wealth left over after his needs. The precondition of repentance is detaching the heart from all existent things and turning it toward the Real, disciplining every limb of the body. It is the forerunner of the fire of hell: weep today with the water of the eyes against what the fire would do tomorrow. And it is a message sent from the Presence:

> O chevalier! How long will you make war? How long will you break the covenant? Come back, make peace! O falcon taken to the sky, come back, don't go! My fingers hold the end of your thread! O free man, how long have you been asleep? Wake up, it is morning, and you are thirsty for the wine of yearning.

### In short

- "In ignorance" covers every sin, deliberate or not, for the Companions agreed that all disobedience is ignorance, as the brothers of Yūsuf were called ignorant though they acted with deliberation.
- "Soon after" reaches to the soul's arrival at the throat, covering virtually the whole of life, except the death-rattle itself, where the next verse takes over.
- Repentance is remorse, quitting, and repair: qada for missed worship, arrears of zakah, rights returned, forgiveness sought.
- The one who repents is loved by Allah, is like one who never sinned, and may even have the record of the sin erased.
- Read inwardly, repentance is the beginning of every happiness, and the Court it leads to is not a court of despair.

18.text:
The companion verse draws the line that the first verse left open: "However, repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying, and then cry, “Now I repent!” nor those who die as disbelievers. For them We have prepared a painful punishment". One verse holds the door open, and this one shows at exactly which moment it closes.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying"** pictures a lifetime spent in fearless disobedience. They had all their years to turn, and wasted every one of them, and only when death stands over them and the withdrawal of the soul has begun do they remember their Lord.

**"and then cry, “Now I repent!”"** is the cry that no longer counts. When hope in continued living has gone, when the soul has reached the throat and is being pulled from the chest, there is no accepted repentance and no way out of that certain end.

**"nor those who die as disbelievers"** extends the refusal beyond the deathbed to the grave. The disbeliever and polytheist who dies as he lived finds that his sorrow and his repentance avail him nothing. Were he to ransom himself with the earth's fill of gold, it would never be taken from him. Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū al-ʿĀliyah said this part was revealed about the people of shirk. One report ties the verse to Tuʾmah and his companions, who had left Islam.

**"For them We have prepared a painful punishment"** is torment that is severe, eternal and enormous.

### Pharaoh at the water

The type of the too-late believer is Pharaoh and his people, who called out while drowning that they believed in the Lord of Mūsā (Moses) and Hārūn (Aaron), and were told that their declaration of faith was of no consequence, because the time set for it was over. The Qur'an records the pattern: "So when they saw Our punishment, they said: We believe in Allah Alone" (40:84). A declaration of faith in the middle of the death-pangs, with the soul being torn from the body, is out of tune with the time and worthless, and no different are the people who wait to confess their sins until the terrors of the Hereafter stand in front of them.

Repentance from the people of the earth will also be refused once the sun rises from the west, for Allah has so decreed: "The day that some of the signs of your Lord do come, no good will it do a person to believe then, if he believed not before, nor earned good through his faith" (6:158).

### The dropping of the veil

The report of Usāmah ibn Salmān from Abū Dharr is recorded by Imam Aḥmad, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> Allah accepts the repentance of His servant, or forgives His servant, as long as the veil does not drop.

They asked what the dropping of the veil meant. He said:

> When the soul is removed while one is a polytheist.

That is the boundary named from Abū Dharr's report, and it matches the limit of the soul-throat hadith collected by at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah. What remains forgivable is decided before that veil drops, and for the children of Ādam (Adam) the door stands open the whole of their lives before it.

### The tongue of learning and the tongue of practice

Read inwardly, the verse distinguishes two tongues. In the tongue of learning, repentance must come before death, even if only by a moment. In the tongue of practice, it must come before the soul takes up the habit of gazing at itself and worshipping itself. Whoever becomes pleased with himself and habitually gazes upon his own glory has had the door of repentance shut in his face and the water of deliverance taken from him. The counsel follows hard: "Quit the companionship of the self-nurturing habit-worshippers, and kiss the dust beneath the feet of those who have disowned self." Not everyone who repents on the road of the sharīʿah and reaches pardon has reached truthfulness in love, and the story of Dāwūd (David) shows the difference. The prophet wept and pleaded for a long time, until it was said to him: "O David, why do you weep, when I have forgiven you, made your adversaries content, and accepted your repentance?" He answered: "Lord God, I know, but give me back those sweet moments I had in Your companionship, and those breaths I had with You in seclusion." The answer came: "David, take heed, that is a love that has passed. From now on, leave the way open for the eyes to weep, for the days of limpidness have no way to return."

### In short

- Repentance is refused at two points: in the pangs of death for the sinner who ignored a lifetime of chances, and at death itself for the disbeliever, whose faith at that moment, like Pharaoh's at the water, comes after the time set for it is over.
- The sun rising from the west will close the door of repentance for everyone on earth.
- The veil drops when the soul leaves the body in polytheism, and before that the servant's whole life is his chance.
- Read inwardly, there is a repentance before the death of the body and a repentance before the death of the heart, and the second door, once the self becomes its own god, is the harder one to reopen.

19.text:
The passage that opened with orphans and inheritance now guards the woman herself: "O believers! It is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will or mistreat them to make them return some of the dowry ˹as a ransom for divorce˺—unless they are found guilty of adultery. Treat them fairly. If you happen to dislike them, you may hate something which Allah turns into a great blessing". Three commands stand in the verse: no inheriting of women, no squeezing of their dowry, and honourable companionship even when the heart has gone cold.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will"** abolishes a practice of the Jāhiliyyah. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said that when a man died, his male relatives held the right to do whatever they pleased with his wife. If one of them wished, he married her, or he passed her in marriage to another man against payment, or barred her from marriage altogether, for they claimed a better right to her than her own family. The verse came down on exactly that.

**"or mistreat them to make them return some of the dowry ˹as a ransom for divorce˺"** forbids the second abuse. The husband is forbidden to use harshness until the woman hands back all or part of her dowry, or surrenders one of her rights under coercion and oppression.

**"unless they are found guilty of adultery"** is the one exception, and its exact width was debated, as the section below shows.

**"Treat them fairly"** is the standing command of companionship, and **"If you happen to dislike them, you may hate something which Allah turns into a great blessing"** forbids the husband to act on dislike alone, since the disliked thing may be carrying a blessing he cannot see.

### The world the verse ended

The root of all the old abuses was one assumption: that a man owned not only the property of the woman but her very life. A woman taken in marriage was passed on, after her husband's death, like a piece of property to his heirs, who became the new owners of the estate and of the widow together. They could take her as a wife themselves, or pass her on to another husband for a payment. The son of the husband from another wife could marry her himself once his father died. From this one social ill grew hundreds of others. Whatever a woman received by inheritance or gift from her parents was devoured by the men of her husband's house. If she did come into possession of property, her relatives by marriage would block any remarriage, so that her share never left the house, and they waited for her to die where she was. A husband who tired of his wife on a whim, with no shortcoming on her side, would neither live with her nor divorce her, but harass her until she returned her jewellery and dower, or forgo the dower still unpaid. Even after divorce, some husbands blocked the woman's remarriage to squeeze the dower out of her.

The verse names the case that stood for all of it. Before Islam, the wife of a deceased father was inherited by the eldest son like any property. The report of the occasion connects it with Kabshah bint Maʿān al-Anṣāriyyah and with Muḥṣin ibn Abī Qays al-Anṣārī. If the inherited woman was rich and beautiful, the son married her without giving any dowry. If she was neither rich nor young nor beautiful, he left her untouched, sometimes for life, unless she ransomed herself with her own money. Allah forbade the practice.

The Qur'an could have used a simple prohibitive order, and instead it said: it is not lawful for you. The negation of lawfulness itself carries a ruling. Should a man proceed to take an adult woman as a wife with no consent and no permission from her, the marriage entered upon is null and void, and no husband-wife relationship is established from it, nor do the injunctions of inheritance or lineage follow from it. Likewise, if a man forces a woman to return the dower or to forgo the outstanding one, a return extracted by force, or a forgiveness forced, counts for nothing in the sight of the sharīʿah, and what is taken that way never becomes lawful, for both are patently ḥarām (forbidden). The word "against their will" is a statement of fact rather than a condition, as al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ notes. A woman in her normal senses would never agree to being owned, and the Islamic law will not concede the position even if some woman, out of her mind, approves of it. What was given to the wife as a gift, or as her own property, cannot be taken back by husband or heirs, though an article lent for temporary use, like jewellery she does not own, remains askable.

### What counts as open lewdness

The exception was read two ways. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and ash-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, Mujāhid with ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam with Abū Ṣāliḥ, as-Suddī and ad-Daḥḥāk, Abū Qilābah, and Ibn Masʿūd with Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Abī Hilāl all said it refers to illicit sex: if the wife commits adultery, the husband may take back the dowry he gave her, and may press her until she returns it in exchange for a khulʿ, a release bought with compensation. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah and ad-Daḥḥāk said the fāḥishah here is disobedience and defiance. In one of the later commentaries, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah and ad-Daḥḥāk are given for disobedience and indecent abuse against the husband, while Abū Qilābah and al-Ḥasan take it as immodesty and adultery in this place. Ibn Jarīr chose the general view: the word covers adultery, disobedience, defiance and rudeness together, so that the husband may press the wife who does any of these until she forfeits all or part of her rights, and then he separates from her. The anchor for the whole discussion stands in Sūrat al-Baqarah: "It is not lawful for you to take back any of what you have given them, except when both parties fear that they would be unable to keep the limits ordained by Allah" (2:229).

### Live with them honourably

The command of companionship was spelled out in practice: kind words, kind treatment, and an appealing appearance, as much as a man can manage, the same as he likes for himself from her. "And they have rights similar over them to what is reasonable" (2:228). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The best among you is he who is the best with his family. Verily, I am the best one among you with my family." His way with his wives was kindness, cheerfulness, play, compassion, spending and laughter. He raced with ʿĀʾishah, the Mother of the Faithful, as a kindness to her. She said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ raced with me and I won the race. This occurred before I gained weight, and afterwards I raced with him again, and he won that race. He said, 'This is for that.'" When he was at the home of one of his wives, sometimes all his wives would meet there and eat together, then return to their homes. He and the wife whose night it was slept in one bed, and he would remove his upper garment and sleep in his lower garment, and he would talk with her after the ʿIshāʾ prayer before sleeping. "Indeed in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example to follow" (33:21). In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim recorded that Jābir said that in the speech the Prophet ﷺ gave at the Farewell Ḥajj he said: "Be kind with women, for you have taken them by Allah's covenant and earned the right to have sexual relations with them by Allah's word."

A deeper justice stands under the command. Property is inanimate, without feeling, and so a proper object of inheritance. A human being has a sensate, independent existence, and so possesses the right to decide her future by her own choice. The widow is not part of the estate to be exploited as the successors decide.

### The disliked wife

The verse ends by holding the husband to patience. Ibn ʿAbbās commented that the husband may come to feel compassion toward a wife he had disliked, and Allah gives him a child with her, and that child carries tremendous goodness. An authentic hadith states: "No believing man should hate his believing wife. If he dislikes a part of her conduct, he would surely like another." One reading of the closing words says plainly that God may provide a righteous child through the very companion whose company the man resents, and the patience of keeping a disliked wife carries reward in this life and the Hereafter. The counsel runs wider than marriage. Living collectively is the condition of human life, and no one survives alone. With tempers differing, irritants crop up, and the only workable approach is to ignore complaints, avoid friction, and give each member of the household the chance to exercise his or her abilities. When one decides to separate instead, one tends to exaggerate the other's faults and fabricate allegations so the weaker party gives ground. That is against the covenant, and a covenant, written or unwritten, is sacred and binds both parties alike.

### The inner reading

Read inwardly, the verse's address is a whole liturgy in itself: the "O" is the call, the "you" the admonishment, the "who have faith" the bearing of witness, and the ruling that follows. Women are considered weak, imprisoned beneath severity, so beware of tormenting them. Neither rule over them through scheming and deceit, nor be severe with them, nor demand of them anything the sharīʿah does not approve. Live with them honourably, by the teachings of the religion and the courtesy of the submitted. Show them the road of the religion, teach them the courteous acts of being Muslim, and protect them from the Fire, as Allah says elsewhere: "Shield yourselves and your families from a Fire" (66:6). Preserve the courtesies of companionship and tolerate suffering from them, but do not lay on them the burden of your service. And though the outward address is to husbands, the allusion reaches every Muslim: never see yourself as having a mandatory due from, or an excellence over, any other Muslim, do not push yourself on those beneath you, and do not use force against the weak, but give them comfort and draw near them. A revelation came to Dāwūd (David): "O David, if you see someone broken in My road, or someone whose heart has been lost in My work, take care to serve him."

### What the passage does next

The surah does not leave the subject here. Verses 20 and 21 tighten the dowry rule from the other side: even a qinṭār, the word whose meaning was given in the commentary on Āl-ʿImrān, may not be reclaimed, a ruling ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb once tested from the minbar with a four-hundred-dirham cap, until a woman of Quraysh stood him down with the Qur'an itself. The two Ṣaḥīḥs then carry the case of the imprecated spouses over the dowry. And the passage closes by sealing one marriage forever: the wife of the father, whose prohibition ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ read as earning the hatred of Allah, and whose violator was dealt with by the mission of Abū Burdah, as the last verse of this group shows. The whole set of rulings is law for this entire ummah, and its shared principle, that the shameful acts named al-fawāḥish are not even to be approached (6:151), runs from the first verse of the group to the last.

### In short

- Women are not estate property. The heirs of a deceased man have no ownership of his widow, and a marriage contracted without the woman's consent is null and void.
- Harassing a wife to recover the dowry is forbidden, with one debated exception: open lewdness, read either as adultery or as defiant disobedience, and the general view covers both.
- Companionship must be honourable, on the pattern of the Prophet's ﷺ own household, from the race he lost and won with ʿĀʾishah to the Farewell Ḥajj command to be kind with women.
- Dislike is not a ground for cruelty, for the disliked wife may carry a blessing, and the believing man is told never to hate her outright.
- Read inwardly, the verse forbids every Muslim to claim excellence over another, and serves the broken in God's road, as Dāwūd was told.

20.text:
The verse of the qinṭār takes the dowry rule to its extreme case: "If you desire to replace a wife with another and you have given the former ˹even˺ a stack of gold ˹as a dowry˺, do not take any of it back. Would you ˹still˺ take it unjustly and very sinfully". The rule is now absolute. Where the previous verse allowed recovery only in the case of the wife's open lewdness, this one removes every excuse based on the size of the amount.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you desire to replace a wife with another"** covers the man who, following his own desire, divorces one wife to marry another in her place, or adds a wife to the one he has. The cause is his wish alone, with no fault on the woman's side.

**"and you have given the former ˹even˺ a stack of gold ˹as a dowry˺"** names the qinṭār, the vast weight of gold, to say that the size of the dowry changes nothing. The verse itself is clear evidence that a dowry may be substantial.

**"do not take any of it back"** is the prohibition, without exception for the amount, and **"Would you ˹still˺ take it unjustly and very sinfully"** is the rebuke. The taking would be calumny and open sin, and the rebuke is meant as a disavowal, not a question.

### Why the claim is an imputation

The logic of the closing words reaches back to verse 19. The only situation in which a husband may claim the dowry back is the wife's shameful act, on the reading the previous verse allowed. So a man who takes it back without that cause is, by his own act, imputing a shameful act to her, and since she has committed none, his claim is a false imputation and an open sin. Where the woman has shown no contumacy and no immodesty, nothing may be claimed from her in exchange for divorce, however much was given, and the dower still outstanding cannot be forced from her either. The shameful acts, the fawāḥish, are of the family of sins the Qur'an commands not even to approach, whether committed openly or secretly (6:151), and unlawful sex itself is named "a Fahishah and an evil way" (17:32). The rights run both ways, for the wives "have rights similar over them to what is reasonable" (2:228), and the exception in Sūrat al-Baqarah stands only where both parties fear they cannot keep the limits of Allah (2:229).

### The caliph corrected

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb used to discourage large dowries, and then changed his view. Imam Aḥmad recorded that Abū al-ʿAjfāʾ as-Sulamī heard ʿUmar say: "Do not exaggerate with the dowry of women." Had the practice been an honour in this world, or a part of taqwā, the Prophet ﷺ would have had more right to it than anyone. Yet: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never gave any of his wives, nor did any of his daughters receive, a dowry more than twelve uqiyyah." Men would sometimes pay a huge dowry precisely to hide enmity toward the wife inside it. Aḥmad and the collectors of the Sunan collected it through various chains, and at-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

Then came the minbar. Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Yaʿlā recorded that Masrūq said that ʿUmar stood on the minbar of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked the people why they exaggerated concerning the dowry, when the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions used to pay up to four hundred dirhams or less. Had paying more been taqwā or honour, they would not have been outdone in it. He said he did not want to hear of a man paying more than four hundred dirhams. Coming down, he was met by a woman of Quraysh who asked whether he had prohibited more than four hundred dirhams in dowry. He said yes. She asked whether he had not heard what Allah sent down, giving a man who has given one of his wives a qinṭār. ʿUmar said: "O Allah, forgive me." He went back up and told the people to pay what they liked of their money. The chain of the hadith is strong. The dowry may be large, and it may not be clawed back.

### The way of the generous

Read inwardly, the verse embodies generosity itself within the religion of friendship, and lays smooth the foundation of chivalry. The counsel given is that cruelty of separation must never be joined to the snatching back of livelihood, for such is not the work of the generous. The scar of separation is already cut into the poor woman's heart, so the hand of her expenditure must not be severed as well, for taking back what was given only lays a second scar upon the first. Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī divorced a wife and then sent her plentiful wealth, saying: "The tribulation of our separation is enough. I must not put upon her the suffering of neediness as well." The wealth was 40,000 dirhams. The woman dumped it on the ground and said: "Paltry goods from a departed lover!" So it is with what is given grudgingly, even a lot of it, after the khulʿ and harassment the earlier verses forbade. The standard for the believing man is the example of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (33:21), whose way with his wives was cheerfulness and spending, and against it the claim on a sinless wife's dowry, with the imputation it carries, stands as far from his way as the case the two Ṣaḥīḥs record of the spouses who imprecated each other, or the closing prohibition on the wives of fathers, whose enforcement was given to Abū Burdah, and the wider list of prohibited women that begins with two sisters in wedlock at the same time (4:23).

### In short

- A husband replacing one wife with another may reclaim nothing of the dowry, not from a qinṭār of gold, for the woman is at no fault.
- The claim without cause is itself an imputation of lewdness, and so a calumny and an open sin.
- ʿUmar capped dowries at four hundred dirhams until a woman of Quraysh corrected him from the Qur'an, and the cap was withdrawn.
- The generous add gifts at separation rather than take back, as Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī did, for the way of the Prophet ﷺ is the standard.

21.text:
The question that ends the argument: "And how could you take it back after having enjoyed each other intimately and she has taken from you a firm commitment". Verse 20 said the taking would be sinful. Verse 21 asks how it is even conceivable.

### Phrase by phrase

**"after having enjoyed each other intimately"** refers to sexual intercourse, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, as-Suddī and several others said. The marriage has been consummated, the couple have come together under one cover, and it is precisely that consummation which makes the dowry due and owned. The word carries more than the act. What has occurred between husband and wife is relationship, love, enjoyment and the sharing of secrets, and greed for the wealth of a woman after all that is shameful as well as forbidden.

**"and she has taken from you a firm commitment"** is the marriage tie itself, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. The covenant is sworn with the name of Allah, witnessed by a gathered company of people, and preceded by a khuṭbah. It is a binding pledge with two branches: that the wife be retained honourably or released with kindness. Through this covenant and the word of Allah she became lawful to her husband, by His decree and His sacred law.

### The case of the imprecated spouses

The two Ṣaḥīḥs record the ruling that fixes what the dowry pays for. In the case of the spouses who pronounced the mutual imprecation, the mulaʿanah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said three times:

> Allah knows that one of you is a liar, so would any of you repent?

The man said: "O Messenger of Allah, my money," meaning the dowry he had given his wife. The Messenger said:

> You have no money. If you are the one who said the truth, the dowry is in return for the right to have sexual relations with her. If you are the one who uttered the lie, then this money is even farther from your reach.

The dowry stands or falls with the consummation the covenant licensed, and the man who destroys the marriage by a lie loses the furthest claim of all.

### The farewell address

Jābir, in the account his Ṣaḥīḥ carries from Muslim, reported that in the speech of the Farewell Ḥajj the Prophet ﷺ said: "Be kind with women, for you have taken them by Allah's covenant and earned the right to have sexual relations with them by Allah's word." The verse and the farewell address say one thing. The right the husband holds was granted by a covenant taken in the name of Allah, and the only fitting response to a covenant of that rank is kindness, not extortion.

### The weight of the covenant

A covenant stands sacred with God. Written or unwritten, it binds in essence, holding the two parties alike and leaving neither free to walk out of it. The command of verse 19 to live with them honourably and the question of verse 21 stand on the same covenant, and the previous verse's allowance, in the single case of the wife's open lewdness, was the exception the law itself drew, not a licence for appetite. Read inwardly, the prior companionship has a firm inviolability, and respect for its due is to stop and keep to what the covenant requires. The Companions understood the gravity. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, the same caliph who yielded on the minbar to the woman of Quraysh, held the marriage covenant in awe, and the household of the Prophet ﷺ, from the race with ʿĀʾishah to the gathering of his wives at one table, modelled what the covenant demands. The passage will close with the severest breach of covenant respect there is, the marriage of a father's wife, an act classed with the fawāḥish that may not even be approached (6:151), with the imputation of the imprecated spouses condemned in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, and with the mission of Abū Burdah against the man who committed it, just before the surah lists the women prohibited forever, beginning with two sisters in wedlock at the same time (4:23), all of it under the same principle of rights held and honoured, "for they have rights similar over them to what is reasonable" (2:228), and the example of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (33:21).

### In short

- The intimacy of marriage is what makes the dowry due, and the covenant of marriage is what made the intimacy lawful. To enjoy both and then reclaim the payment is theft from one's own oath.
- In the imprecation case the Prophet ﷺ ruled that the dowry is the price of the consummated right, and the lying spouse has no claim on it at all.
- The Farewell Ḥajj address names the covenant of Allah as what grants the husband's right, and kindness as its only fitting use.
- The covenant binds both parties, and its gravity is the measure of every breach, from dowry extortion to the marriage of a father's wife.

22.text:
The passage on women closes its first movement with a prohibition that restores the honour of fatherhood: "Do not marry former wives of your fathers—except what was done previously. It was indeed a shameful, despicable, and evil practice". One sentence ends a practice of the Jāhiliyyah and stamps it with three names of condemnation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not marry former wives of your fathers"** prohibits the women whom the father married, in honour and respect to the fathers, so that no son may ever approach the wife of his father, in the father's lifetime or after his death. As soon as the father's marriage contract is conducted, the woman is closed to the son of her husband, on which ruling the scholars hold consensus. The prohibition needs no consummation by the father to take effect.

**"except what was done previously"** forgives what happened in the time of ignorance before Islam. The maxim that the past is past applies: orders based on things now irrelevant breed endless problems, so the past is left to Allah and the present reformed.

**"It was indeed a shameful, despicable, and evil practice"** gives the three weights of the act. Shameful, an obscenity. Despicable, the word maqtan: offensive and hated. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said it means Allah will hate him who does it. And an evil way, the worst path to follow.

### The world it closed

During the Jāhiliyyah the people prohibited what Allah prohibits concerning marriage, except in two matters: marrying the stepmother, and taking two sisters as rival wives. Ibn Jarīr recorded that from Ibn ʿAbbās, and similar reports come from ʿAṭāʾ and Qatādah. This verse and the next closed both: "And marry not women whom your fathers married," and "and two sisters in wedlock at the same time" (4:23). How can someone keep calling a woman his mother for years and then stoop to make her his wife once the father dies? The act is itself a sin, and it breeds hate, for a man who marries a woman tends to resent whoever was married to her before him, and this sin teaches the son to resent his own father. The same logic protects the Mothers of the Faithful, who were not allowed to any man after the Messenger ﷺ. He is as a father to the believers, and far more, and his right comes before each person's love of himself. The act belongs to the family of sins the Qur'an fences off entirely: "Come not near to al-Fawāḥish (shameful acts) whether committed openly or secretly" (6:151), and "And come not near to unlawful sex. Verily, it is a Fahishah and an evil way" (17:32).

### The occasions

Several cases were named with the verse's revelation. Hisn ibn Abī al-Qays took as wife Kubayshah bint Maʿān, who had been his father's wife. Al-Aswad ibn Khalaf married the wife of his father. Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah married his father's wife Fakhītah bint al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib. Manẓūr ibn Zabbān married the wife of his father Mulaykah bint Khārijah. And Ashʿat ibn Sawār told of the case that brought the question: Abū Qays, one of the righteous people of Madinah, died, and his son Qays proposed to his father's wife. She said to him: "But I consider you like my son. I will consult the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, to see what he commands." She went and informed him, and Allah revealed this verse. Another report names the verse's subject as Muḥṣin ibn Abī Qays al-Anṣārī.

### The punishment

The offence was treated as reversion from the religion. Those who commit this practice deserve capital punishment and confiscation of their property, which is given to the Muslim treasury. Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, in a report Aḥmad and the Sunan collectors carry, told how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ despatched his uncle Abū Burdah to a man who had married his stepmother, with orders to execute him and confiscate his money. The verse was law for the whole ummah, and the law was enforced.

### Rulings from the verse

The verse introduces the muḥarramāt, the women prohibited in marriage, whose list the coming verses will give in full. Some are prohibited forever, by kinship, by fosterage, or by relationship through marriage, and never become lawful under any condition. Others are prohibited only until they are bound in marriage with someone else. From this verse the jurists drew its edges both ways. The bare fact that the father married a woman forbids her to the son, with no need for consummation. By the same principle the father may not take the wife of his son, even where the son's marriage went no further than the formal nikāḥ, with the wife not yet having come to live with him. Whoever holds to taqwā holds to the limits of respect the verse guards.

### The inner reading

Read inwardly, the verse alludes to the protection of honour and staying within the limits of respect. Since a man naturally hates that another should bed his wife, sons are barred from trampling the father's rights in pursuit of the father's wife. The same jealousy of honour, turned upward, is why the believers' mothers were sealed after the Prophet ﷺ, whose example the Qur'an commands: "Indeed in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example to follow" (33:21). And the covenant-honour of this whole passage, from verse 19 through the farewell address recorded by Muslim from Jābir at the Ḥajj, to the dowry ruling of the two Ṣaḥīḥs, reaches its peak here, for the father's bed is the first covenant of all.

### In short

- The wife of one's father is prohibited by the marriage contract alone, forever, and the father's wife is equally closed to no son by any device of the Jāhiliyyah.
- The prohibition was new law for the ummah: the pre-Islamic custom that allowed it, along with rival sisters, was ended, the past forgiven.
- The act is obscene, hated by Allah, and an evil way, classed among the fawāḥish not even to be approached, and it was punished in this world by execution and confiscation, as Abū Burdah's mission shows.
- The verse opens the surah's list of prohibited women and guards, above all, the honour of the father and the sanctity of the covenant.

23.text:
The verse of the muḥarramāt, the women prohibited in marriage: "˹Also˺ forbidden to you for marriage are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal and maternal aunts, your brother's daughters, your sister's daughters, your foster-mothers, your foster-sisters, your mothers-in-law, your stepdaughters under your guardianship if you have consummated marriage with their mothers—but if you have not, then you can marry them—nor the wives of your own sons, nor two sisters together at the same time—except what was done previously. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful". One verse closes a whole map of relationships, by blood, by suckling and by marriage, and it ends with forgiveness for what the past had already allowed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"your mothers, your daughters, your sisters"** opens with the closest degrees. Mothers includes every grandmother, paternal or maternal. Daughters includes the daughter's daughter and the son's daughter, down the line. Sisters covers the full sister, the ʿallātī sister of the same father, and the akhyaḳī sister of the same mother. A daughter born of zinā follows the rule of the daughter, and marriage with her is not correct, just as a stepdaughter from a different husband has her own rule further in the verse. Adopted children, by contrast, are not blood, and it is permissible to marry them or their offspring, provided nothing else prohibits it. Even where a father has fallen into illicit relations with a woman, his son may still not marry her.

**"your paternal and maternal aunts"** closes the aunts in full. The father's sister is prohibited, whether she is his full sister or a half-sister from either side, and the same holds for the mother's sister. The readings extend both to great-aunts, the sisters of grandfathers and grandmothers.

**"your brother's daughters, your sister's daughters"** takes in the nieces, again whether the brother or sister is full, ʿallātī or akhyaḳī, and the children of these daughters follow them into prohibition.

**"your foster-mothers, your foster-sisters"** builds a second family out of milk, with the same force as the first, as the sections below unfold.

**"your mothers-in-law"** prohibits the wife's mother from the moment the marriage contract exists, consummated or not, and the word mothers there includes all the wife's grandmothers, maternal, paternal, lineal or foster.

**"your stepdaughters under your guardianship if you have consummated marriage with their mothers"** gives the rule of the rabība, the wife's daughter by another husband: prohibited once the husband has consummated the marriage with her mother, with her granddaughters included in the prohibition. **"but if you have not, then you can marry them"** is the mercy at its centre: where the marriage was contracted but never consummated, the stepdaughter remains lawful.

**"nor the wives of your own sons"** prohibits the daughter-in-law, and the word sons reaches to grandsons, paternal or maternal, with a decisive restriction examined below: from your own loins, which excludes the adopted son.

**"nor two sisters together at the same time"** bars the rival sisters, real or half, by lineage or by suckling.

**"except what was done previously"** forgives the marriages of the Jāhiliyyah, and **"Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** promises that what people did erroneously before Islam will be overlooked once they have embraced it.

### Seven by blood, seven by marriage

Ibn ʿAbbās counted the verse's work in two sevens. Allah has prohibited seven types of relatives by blood and seven by marriage, he said, and then recited this verse. At-Ṭabarī recorded the saying, and the count itself is a summary of the map: mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, brother's daughters, sister's daughters, then the second seven built by milk and by contract.

### What suckling establishes

The milk-relationship is not a metaphor. ʿĀʾishah, the Mother of the Faithful, is the narrator, in the records of al-Bukhārī and Muslim alike, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Suckling prohibits what birth prohibits." In another narration reported by Muslim: "Suckling establishes prohibited degrees just as blood does." The woman who suckles a child becomes his foster-mother, her husband his foster-father, her children his brothers and sisters, her sisters his maternal aunts, her husband's brothers and sisters his foster-uncles and paternal aunts, and marriage is prohibited across the whole map exactly as it is by kinship.

How much suckling establishes it was itself once recited. In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim recorded that ʿĀʾishah said that among the parts of the Qur'an that were revealed was the statement: "Ten incidents of suckling establishes the prohibition concerning marriage." Five later replaced the ten, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away with the statement still recited as part of the Qur'an. Sahlah bint Suhayl narrates the application: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told her to give Sālim, the freed slave of Abū Hudhayfah, five sucklings. Less than five incidents of suckling will not establish the prohibition.

The timing matters. The suckling must occur within the usual days of suckling, before the age of two, as the Qur'an sets the term: "The mothers should suckle their children for two whole years" (2:233), the rule explained in Sūrat al-Baqarah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Fosterage is only from hunger," meaning it counts where the child has no option but to suckle and grow through it, recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim. According to Imam Abū Ḥanīfah the period runs from birth to two and a half years. According to other jurists, among them his special disciples Imam Abū Yūsuf and Imam Muḥammad, the period is two years only, and suckling after the age of two establishes no prohibition.

The jurists drew out the working rules. Two children suckled by one woman cannot marry each other, and the daughter of a foster-brother or foster-sister is equally closed. The lineal mother of a foster-brother remains lawful, as does the foster-mother of the lineal sister of a foster-sister. The feed counts if received through the mouth or the nose in the days of suckling, but not through any other inlet, and milk of animals or of a man establishes nothing. Where a woman's feed is mixed into medicine or animal milk, the prohibition stands only if her milk is the greater part or at least equal. If a man's glands were ever to lactate, it proves nothing. Mere mouthing at the breast without certainty of a feed establishes no prohibition, for the law is not built on a doubt. Where a woman claims after a marriage that she suckled both spouses, the claim confirmed by both dissolves the marriage, while a claim rejected by both leaves it standing, though the God-fearing pair would do well to separate. Proof needs two practicing Muslim witnesses, one man and two women equalling two men, and given that a whole life turns ḥalāl or ḥarām on it, the prudent course is to hold back from the marriage even on a single upright witness's word.

### The mother-in-law and the stepdaughter

The mother of the wife is prohibited by the contract alone. Even if the husband never slept with his wife, her mother is unlawful for him to marry, and the rule runs wider. The mother of a woman with whom a man slept in the belief she was his wife, though she was not, and the mother of a woman with whom he committed zinā, or whom he touched lustfully, is equally unlawful to him.

The stepdaughter's rule turns on consummation. When a man marries a woman and sleeps with her after the nikāh, the woman's daughter from another husband becomes unlawful for him, and with her the daughter's granddaughters on both sides. If he has not slept with the wife and then divorces her after the contract, her daughter and granddaughter remain lawful for him. And consummation is read broadly: a lustful touch after the nikāḥ, or a look at her private part with desire, is taken as having had relations with her, and closes the daughter.

The words "your women" are general. It is not the legally wedded wife only whose daughters become unlawful, but any woman with whom the man has had intercourse, in marriage, in the mistaken belief she was his wife, or in zinā. The daughter and granddaughter of such a woman are closed to him.

### The stepdaughter hadith

Whether the stepdaughter was under the stepfather's guardianship makes no difference. The majority of scholars state that the stepdaughter is prohibited for the stepfather who consummated the marriage with her mother, guardianship or no guardianship, and the Prophet's ﷺ own case settles it. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Umm Ḥabībah said: "O Messenger of Allah, marry my sister, the daughter of Abū Sufyān," named in one narration as ʿAzzah bint Abū Sufyān. He asked: "Do you like that I do that?" She said she would not give him up for anything, but the best person she liked to share with her in righteous good was her sister. He said: "That is not allowed for me." She said they had been told that he wanted to marry the daughter of Abū Salamah. He asked: "The daughter of Umm Salamah?" She said yes. He said: "Even if she was not my stepdaughter and under my guardianship, she would still not be allowed for me." The reason lay in milk: she was his niece through suckling, for Thuwaybah had nursed him and Abū Salamah both. He closed the matter with the words: "Therefore, do not offer me to marry your daughters or sisters." In another narration: "Had I not married Umm Salamah, her daughter would not have been allowed for me anyway." His marriage to Umm Salamah was the real reason behind the prohibition, and the foster-tie reinforced it.

### Sons' wives, and the adopted

The wife of one's own son is prohibited, and the universality of "sons" includes grandsons, paternal or maternal. The restriction "from your own loins" excludes the adopted son, for adoption was a common practice of the Jāhiliyyah, and the wife of an adopted son is lawful to marry once he has released her. Allah said: "So when Zayd had accomplished his desire from her, We gave her to you in marriage, so that there may be no difficulty to the believers in respect of the wives of their adopted sons, when the latter have no desire to keep them" (33:37).

Ibn Jurayj said he asked ʿAṭāʾ about this part of the verse, and was told that the Prophet's ﷺ marriage to the former wife of Zayd, his adopted son before Islam ended the practice, drew criticism from the idolators of Makkah. Allah then sent down the verse on wives of sons born of one's own loins, together with "nor has He made your adopted sons your real sons" (33:4), and "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men" (33:40). Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad said these verses are encompassing, covering the wives of the sons and the wives' mothers whether the marriage was consummated or not, and there is consensus on that ruling. The same explanation is given by Ṭāwūs, Ibrāhīm, az-Zuhrī and Makhūl.

One question remained. Why is the wife of a son by suckling prohibited, when there is no blood? The answer is the Prophet's ﷺ word already cited: suckling prohibits what birth prohibits.

### Two sisters together

No one may take or keep two sisters as rival wives, or as rival female-servants, according to the consensus of the Companions' scholars, their followers and the Imams of old and present. The sisters may be real, ʿallātī or akhyaḳī, by lineage or by suckling. Where one sister has been divorced, marrying the other becomes permissible only after her ʿiddah, the waiting period, has expired. The sunnah adds the aunts: it is not lawful to combine a woman with her paternal aunt, nor with her maternal aunt, as reported in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, where the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not combine a woman with her paternal aunt, nor a woman with her maternal aunt." The jurists state the general principle: any two women who, were one of them a male, could not lawfully marry each other, cannot be combined in marriage with one man. Each of them may be married separately, and handmaidens may be owned together, but the bed is shared with only one at a time.

### The exception of the past

Whatever happened in the Jāhiliyyah is not called to account. The words appeared in the previous verse and appear again here: what came to pass then has passed, and the one who embraces Islam is not judged by it, though he must leave the practice now. That included separation. Whoever held the wife of his father, or two sisters, in marriage at the coming of Islam had to part from them, one sister necessarily being divorced. A man who had married his father's wife was, as al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib narrated, executed on the Prophet's ﷺ order, the mission going to Abū Burdah ibn Niyār. And the converts came with their own cases. Ad-Daḥḥāk bin Fayruz, in a report Imam Aḥmad carries, said that his father told him: "I embraced Islam while married to two sisters at the same time, and the Prophet ﷺ commanded me to divorce one of them." Ibn Firoz ad-Dailamī narrates from his father the same ruling in his own words: "When I embraced Islam, I had two sisters married to me. I went to the Prophet ﷺ with the problem. He said: 'Separate by divorcing one and keeping the other.'" The same reaching back is the verse's own closing: Allah is Forgiving of what people did in the pre-Islamic era, and Merciful regarding what ensues from them in Islam, provided they repent.

### Why the limits at all

The verse answers a human fact. Desires make themselves felt in people, sexuality among them, and the Islamic law, which fixes a limit for every emotion, fixes the limits of sexual alliance too. Only the alliance established through a standard, solemn social agreement, which is marriage, is valid, and the family life it builds must carry an environment of chastity. For that purpose, the closest relations are declared prohibited, kept beyond and above sexual desire, so that a zone of the household remains forever free of it, where trust needs no guard.

### The inner reading

Read inwardly, the verse teaches how the believer stands before the law at all. The sharīʿah rests on servanthood, not on self-exertion. Its canon comes by transmission, not by rational derivation, and the sunnah stands on surrender, not on the hunting for reasons. Surrender is an easy road, a flourishing dwelling, and its goal is the approval of the All-Merciful. Self-exertion and self-determination make a hard road through ruins, ending in what is unwholesome. So leap clear of self-exertion's road and cling to surrender, and quit the search for causes. Whatever the sharīʿah has declared forbidden, consider forbidden, a consignment by the Desire built on the Will. Had the same thing been permitted instead, the surrender would be the same, for He is the Real, majestic in His majesty, who "does whatsoever He wills" (3:40) and "decrees whatsoever He desires" (5:1). To whom He wills He forbids, and to whom He wills He allows. His craftsmanship is without cause, His decree without protester.

### In short

- Seven degrees of blood and seven of marriage are closed forever: the direct line up and down, the sisters, the aunts on both sides, the nieces, and, by milk and by contract, their counterparts.
- Suckling prohibits what birth prohibits, once it passes the threshold of five feeds within the suckling age, two years by the dominant reckoning, and its whole family map follows.
- The mother-in-law is prohibited by the contract alone. The stepdaughter, by consummation with her mother, broadly read to include the lustful touch. The daughter-in-law, by the marriage of one's own son, adopted sons excluded by the Qur'an's own ruling.
- Two sisters, and a woman with her aunt, may not be combined in one marriage, and the converts of the Jāhiliyyah were ordered to release what they held.
- The believer receives the list in surrender, for the law is transmitted, not bargained over, and its Maker decrees what He desires.

24.text:
The map of prohibited marriages closes, and the verse turns to what remains: "Also ˹forbidden are˺ married women—except ˹female˺ captives in your possession. This is Allah's commandment to you. Lawful to you are all beyond these—as long as you seek them with your wealth in a legal marriage, not in fornication. Give those you have consummated marriage with their due dowries. It is permissible to be mutually gracious regarding the set dowry. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise". One sentence forbids, one opens, one commands the dower, and one permits graciousness after it is fixed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Also ˹forbidden are˺ married women"** adds the married woman to the list. So long as a woman is bound to a husband, no other man may marry her. From this the verse settles, on its face, that a woman cannot live with more than one husband at a time.

**"except ˹female˺ captives in your possession"** makes the one exception, women acquired through war, as the sections below explain.

**"This is Allah's commandment to you"** means the prohibition was ordained by Allah, and the believer's part is to adhere to His Book, never to transgress His set limits, the ḥudūd, and to hold to His legislation and decrees.

**"Lawful to you are all beyond these"** opens everything not prohibited: the cousins on either side of the family, an uncle's wife once he has died or divorced her, the wife of an adopted son once he releases her, and, after one's wife has died, even her sister, provided no other bar exists.

**"as long as you seek them with your wealth in a legal marriage, not in fornication"** sets the method. A man may use his money to marry up to four wives, and for as many bondwomen as lawfully come to him, all through lawful means. The purpose named is chastity, the guarding of modesty, and not the spending of wealth on women for zinā. The fornicator also spends from his assets, but that spending is patently unlawful, and a woman procured by it never becomes lawful to enjoy.

**"Give those you have consummated marriage with their due dowries"** makes the dower an obligation once the marriage is enjoyed. **"It is permissible to be mutually gracious regarding the set dowry"** allows, after the duty is settled, an increase from the husband or a willing forfeiture from the wife.

**"Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"** closes with the two names that govern everything before them.

### The occasion at Awtas

The exception was revealed over a real scruple. Imam Aḥmad recorded that Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said:

> We captured some women from the area of Awtas who were already married, and we disliked having sexual relations with them because they already had husbands. So we asked the Prophet ﷺ about this matter, and this verse was revealed: "Also forbidden are married women, except those whom your right hands possess." Consequently, we had sexual relations with these women.

At-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr and Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ collected it in this wording. The fuller reports tell of the day of Hunayn, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent an army to Awtas, which met the enemy, defeated them and took many female prisoners. Some of the Companions were uncomfortable, for the women had husbands who were idolaters. In one version they said plainly: "O Prophet of Allah! How can we possibly have physical relationships with women whose lineage and husband we know very well?" And the verse came down.

The rule the verse carries is careful. Such women came into Muslim hands when jihād had to be carried out against the infidels of Dār al-Ḥarb, and they are lawful only after it is certain they are not pregnant, by waiting for the lapse of one menstruation, and if pregnancy appears, by waiting until the child is delivered.

### Why one husband and not several

Some ignorant and loudmouthed people in later times took the permission of plurality for wives to mean that women should equally enjoy several husbands. The verse answers them before they were born. A woman with more than one husband at once is not only a burden on herself and a disgrace to the men, it destroys lineage itself: when many men share one woman, no method remains of attributing the fatherhood of the child to any one of them, and when lineage goes unproved, who is charged with the mutual rights and duties of parents and children? Even on nature and reason alone, the case fails. The basic purpose of marriage is procreation, and several women can conceive from one man, while one woman conceives from one man only, so the procreative power of all the husbands but one is wasted. The woman is the more delicate, and there are long stretches and many conditions in which she cannot fulfil the rights of one husband, let alone several. And where a man's strength is above average, restriction to one wife drives him into impermissible ways that ruin society, a ruination hardly to be feared from the woman's side.

The law goes further than the moment. A divorced or widowed woman may not marry another until her ʿiddah, the waiting period, has expired. And where the wife embraces Islam while her husband remains a disbeliever in Dār al-Ḥarb, the non-Muslim land at war, she is released from the bond after three menstrual periods. Where she embraces Islam in Dār al-Islām, the legal authority induces the husband toward Islam, and if he refuses, the judge effects a separation that counts as a divorce, after which she completes her ʿiddah and may marry whom she chooses.

### What remains lawful, and the limit of four

The permission "all beyond these" is wide but not unmeasured. It is not permissible to have more than four wives at once, a ruling the surah has already given, and the absence of the number here should mislead no one into reading the generality as unrestricted. Beyond the women the Qur'an itself prohibits, the sunnah prohibits others, such as a woman together with her aunt, and the books of fiqh gather them all.

### The dower

Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ, in his Aḥkām al-Qur'ān, draws two rulings from the words "seek them with your wealth". First, marriage cannot stand without a dower. Even if the parties agree between themselves on a marriage without one, the dower remains necessary. Second, the mahr must be māl, wealth of some kind, property or assets. According to the Ḥanafiyyah it should not be less than ten dirhams, a dirham being equivalent to 17 grains Troy of silver.

The phrase "those you have consummated marriage with" was read by the entire ummah, from the revered early elders to their successors, as coition. The full dower falls due only when the husband has had that benefit of the marriage. If the contract was made but the wife never came to live with him and he divorces before consummation, half the mahr is due. Once the benefit has been received, any shortcoming in payment is against the letter and spirit of the law, and honour itself says the wife's due should not be delayed. The sharīʿah adds her weapon: where the dower is prompt, she may refuse to go to her husband until it is paid. The whole rule hangs on the Qur'an's own words: "It is not lawful for you to take back any of what you have given them" (2:229).

### The mutʿah question

Mujāhid stated that "those you have consummated marriage with" was revealed about the mutʿah, the temporary marriage that ends on a predetermined date, and a later sect built on that reading a claim that mutʿah is ḥalāl. The claim fails inside the verse itself. The Qur'an allows the seeking of women only "in a legal marriage, not in fornication", binding oneself in wedlock and not only for lust, and the relationship it approves is the one that aims at chastity through the permanent bond.
